lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Pouring gold is the step where your hard-won smelted gold finally becomes a sellable product. In Africa, most small-scale miners and refiners sell their gold as raw dust or impure nuggets, earning 70-85% of the global price. If you pour clean, uniform bars or buttons, you can sell directly to jewelers, banks, or international buyers at 95-98% of spot price. For example, a 1kg bar of 99% purity sells for about $60,000 USD, while the same gold as dust might fetch only $45,000. That difference is your profit.

Pouring also protects you from theft and fraud. A solid bar is easy to weigh, test, and store. Buttons (small round discs) are perfect for local markets where buyers want 10g, 20g, or 50g pieces. In countries like Ghana, Tanzania, and South Africa, licensed gold buyers require bars with a stamped weight and purity. Without proper pouring, you cannot access these better-paying markets.

This module teaches you to melt and pour gold safely using simple tools: a furnace, graphite crucibles, borax, and steel molds. You will learn to make both large bars (100g to 1kg) and small buttons (5g to 50g). We focus on practical methods that work in a small workshop with limited electricity. By the end, you will be able to produce gold bars that look professional and pass a buyer's inspection.

Remember: pouring is not just about melting metal. It is about controlling temperature, removing impurities, and creating a smooth surface. A poorly poured bar with cracks or slag will be rejected or heavily discounted. A well-poured bar speaks for itself. This module will give you the skills to pour with confidence and increase your income.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To pour gold bars and buttons, you need a few essential tools. First, a furnace that can reach 1,200Â°C. In Africa, many use a simple charcoal furnace with a blower, but a propane or electric furnace is cleaner and easier to control. For small-scale work, a 1kg crucible furnace costs about $200-$500. Second, crucibles: graphite or clay-graphite crucibles are best. They handle thermal shock and do not react with gold. Buy at least two: one for melting, one as backup. A 1kg crucible costs $10-$20.

Third, molds. For bars, use steel or cast iron molds. They must be clean, dry, and preheated to 200Â°C before pouring. You can buy professional ingot molds online for $50-$150, or make your own from thick steel plates clamped together. For buttons, use a carbon mold with multiple round depressions, or simply pour into a bucket of water to make shot (but buttons are better for local sales). Fourth, safety gear: leather apron, face shield, heat-resistant gloves, and proper ventilation. Do not skip these.

Fifth, flux. Borax (sodium borate) is the most common. It absorbs impurities and helps the gold flow. You can buy borax at any market or chemical shop for $2 per kg. Also, have a small amount of soda ash or silica sand for stubborn slag. Sixth, a torch or kiln for preheating molds. A propane torch works fine. Seventh, a digital scale (0.1g accuracy) and a set of tongs long enough to reach into the furnace.

Finally, a clean, flat surface to work on. Never pour on concrete or wet groundâmoisture causes explosions. Use a steel plate or dry sand bed. Keep a bucket of dry sand nearby to smother spills. With these tools, you are ready to pour safely and efficiently. Total startup cost: $300-$800, which pays back after selling just a few bars.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Prepare your workspace. Clear a 2-meter area. Place your furnace on a steel plate. Ensure good ventilationâopen doors or use a fan. Put on your safety gear. Preheat your mold to 200Â°C using a torch. A cold mold causes gold to splatter and stick.

Step 2: Melt the gold. Weigh your gold dust or nuggets. For every 100g of gold, add 5g of borax. Put the gold and borax into a preheated crucible. Place the crucible in the furnace. Heat to 1,100-1,200Â°C. Gold melts at 1,064Â°C. Watch for a bright orange, liquid pool. Stir gently with a graphite rod to mix the flux. Skim off any slag that floats to the top using a steel spoon. Do not overheatâabove 1,300Â°C, gold evaporates and you lose money.

Step 3: Pour the gold. Once the gold is fully liquid and slag-free, remove the crucible with long tongs. Hold the crucible close to the mold (2-3 cm away). Tilt slowly and steadily. Pour in one continuous motion. Do not stop and startâthat creates lines and bubbles. For a bar, fill the mold to the top. For buttons, pour into each depression quickly. The gold should flow like honey. If it is too thick, add a pinch more borax and reheat for 30 seconds.

Step 4: Cool and remove. Let the mold sit for 2-3 minutes. The gold will turn from orange to red to dull yellow. Do not quench in waterâit can crack the bar. Once solid, turn the mold upside down and tap gently. The bar should drop out. If it sticks, reheat the mold slightly.

Step 5: Clean and finish. Scrub the bar with a wire brush and warm soapy water to remove borax residue. For a shiny finish, dip in a 10% sulfuric acid solution for 30 seconds, then rinse. Weigh and stamp the bar with its weight and purity (e.g., 100g, 999). Your gold is now ready for sale.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Pouring wet or cold molds. Moisture in a mold turns to steam and explodes, sending molten gold everywhere. Fix: Always preheat molds to 200Â°C. If you see steam or hear a hiss, stop and reheat.

Mistake 2: Too much or too little borax. Too little, and slag stays in the gold, making it brittle. Too much, and the gold becomes thick and hard to pour. Fix: Use 5g borax per 100g gold. If the melt looks cloudy, add 1g more. If it looks like syrup, you added too muchâskim it off.

Mistake 3: Overheating. Gold above 1,300Â°C starts to evaporate and you lose weight. Also, the crucible wears out faster. Fix: Use a pyrometer or watch the color. Bright yellow-white is too hot. Orange is perfect. If you see fumes, turn down the heat.

Mistake 4: Pouring too fast or too slow. Fast pouring splashes and creates bubbles. Slow pouring causes the gold to cool and clog. Fix: Practice with water first. Pour in a steady stream, like pouring cooking oil. Keep the crucible close to the mold.

Mistake 5: Not skimming slag. Slag on top of the melt will end up in your bar, creating dark spots and weak spots. Fix: Always skim before pouring. Use a steel spoon or graphite rod. If slag keeps forming, add a pinch of soda ash.

Mistake 6: Using the wrong mold material. Iron molds can contaminate gold with rust. Fix: Use steel, cast iron, or carbon molds. Never use aluminum or copper. Clean molds after each use.

Mistake 7: Quenching in water. This makes the bar crack and become brittle. Fix: Let it air cool. If you must speed up cooling, place the mold on a dry sand bed.

Mistake 8: Not weighing and stamping. Buyers need to know weight and purity. Fix: Use a digital scale and a steel stamp set. Stamp clearly on the bar's face.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety is not optional when pouring gold. Molten gold is 1,100Â°Câit will burn through skin, clothes, and shoes in seconds. In Africa, many small-scale accidents happen because miners skip protective gear. Do not be one of them.

First, wear the right gear: a leather apron, long leather gloves, a face shield (not just goggles), and closed leather boots. Cotton clothes can catch fire; wear wool or leather. Tie back long hair. Never wear synthetic fabrics like nylonâthey melt onto skin.

Second, ventilation. Gold smelting releases toxic fumes: metal oxides, flux fumes, and possibly lead or mercury if your gold is dirty. Work outdoors or in a shed with a fan blowing fumes away from you. Never smelt in a closed room. If you feel dizzy or have a headache, stop and get fresh air.

Third, fire safety. Keep a dry powder fire extinguisher nearby. Never use water on a gold fireâit causes explosions. Keep a bucket of dry sand to smother small fires. Clear your workspace of any flammable materials: paper, cloth, petrol, or solvents.

Fourth, handle crucibles with care. Hot crucibles can crack if dropped. Use long tongs and never touch a crucible with bare hands. Let crucibles cool slowlyâdo not dip in water. Inspect crucibles for cracks before each use. A cracked crucible can spill molten gold.

Fifth, best practice for quality. Always preheat molds. Use clean gold and fresh borax. Pour in one smooth motion. Let bars cool slowly. Clean and stamp every bar. Keep a logbook of each pour: date, weight in, weight out, purity, and any issues. This helps you improve and shows buyers you are professional.

Finally, work with a partner. Never pour alone. If an accident happens, someone can call for help. Teach your partner first aid for burns: cool the burn with clean water for 20 minutes, cover with a sterile cloth, and go to a clinic. Remember, a safe refiner is a profitable refiner.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
This exercise will guide you through pouring a 50g gold button and a 100g gold bar. You will need: 150g of clean gold dust or nuggets (or scrap gold), a furnace, two graphite crucibles, borax, a steel bar mold, a carbon button mold, tongs, a digital scale, and safety gear.

Step 1: Set up. Put on all safety gear. Place furnace on a steel plate in a well-ventilated area. Preheat both molds to 200Â°C with a torch. Weigh 150g of gold. Divide into two lots: 50g for buttons, 100g for a bar.

Step 2: Melt the button gold. Put 50g gold and 2.5g borax in a crucible. Heat to 1,150Â°C. Stir with a graphite rod. Skim slag. Pour into the carbon button mold in one steady stream. Let cool for 3 minutes. Remove the button. It should be round and shiny. Weigh it. You should have about 49g (1g lost to slag and handling). Record the weight.

Step 3: Melt the bar gold. Put 100g gold and 5g borax in a clean crucible. Heat to 1,150Â°C. Stir and skim. Pour into the steel bar mold. Fill to the top. Let cool for 5 minutes. Remove the bar. It should be rectangular and smooth. Weigh it. Expect about 98g. Clean with a wire brush and soapy water. If you want a shiny finish, dip in 10% sulfuric acid for 30 seconds, then rinse.

Step 4: Stamp and evaluate. Use a steel stamp to mark the weight and purity (e.g.,

). Check for defects: cracks, bubbles, or slag spots. If you see defects, note them. A good bar has a smooth surface and sharp edges. If your bar has bubbles, you poured too fast or the mold was too cold. If it has slag spots, you did not skim enough.

Step 5: Repeat. Do this exercise three times. Each time, try to reduce weight loss and improve surface quality. Keep a logbook. After three pours, you should be able to produce a bar that a buyer will accept without discount. This skill will directly increase your income.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of selling poured gold bars instead of raw gold dust?
options: A) Bars are easier to transport
B) Bars sell for 95-98% of spot price versus 70-85% for dust
D) Bars do not need weighing
quiz.explanation: Poured bars command a higher price because they are uniform and easier to assay.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to absorb impurities during gold melting?
quiz.explanation: Borax is the most common flux that absorbs impurities and helps gold flow.

quiz.q: What is the melting point of gold?
quiz.explanation: Gold melts at 1,064Â°C, but it is often heated to 1,100-1,200Â°C for pouring.

quiz.q: Why must molds be preheated before pouring gold?
options: A) To make the gold flow faster
B) To prevent steam explosions and splattering
C) To change the gold's color
quiz.explanation: Moisture in a cold mold turns to steam and can cause explosive splattering of molten gold.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of borax per 100g of gold?
quiz.explanation: 5g of borax per 100g of gold is the standard ratio for effective fluxing.

quiz.q: What happens if you overheat gold above 1,300Â°C?
options: B) It evaporates and you lose gold
quiz.explanation: Gold evaporates at very high temperatures, causing weight loss and financial loss.

quiz.q: Which mold material is NOT recommended for pouring gold?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum can contaminate gold and has a low melting point, making it unsafe.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after pouring gold into a mold?
options: B) Let it air cool for 2-3 minutes
quiz.explanation: Air cooling prevents cracking and brittleness that can occur with water quenching.

quiz.q: Why is it important to skim slag before pouring?
options: A) To make the gold lighter
B) To prevent slag from ending up in the bar
D) To change the gold's color
quiz.explanation: Slag on the surface can mix into the bar, creating weak spots and impurities.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to pour gold into a mold?
options: A) Pour quickly in short bursts
B) Pour slowly in one continuous stream
C) Pour from a height of 30 cm
quiz.explanation: A steady, continuous pour close to the mold prevents bubbles and lines.

quiz.q: Which safety gear is essential when pouring gold?
options: B) Face shield and leather apron
quiz.explanation: A face shield and leather apron protect against molten gold splashes and heat.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy while smelting?
options: B) Drink water and keep going
C) Stop and get fresh air
quiz.explanation: Dizziness indicates toxic fume exposure; you must stop and get fresh air immediately.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to use water on a gold fire?
options: A) It makes the fire hotter
quiz.explanation: Water on molten gold causes a steam explosion that can spray molten metal.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a logbook in gold pouring?
options: A) To record weight in, weight out, purity, and issues
quiz.explanation: A logbook helps you improve your technique and shows professionalism to buyers.

quiz.q: How much weight loss is typical when pouring a 100g gold bar?
quiz.explanation: About 2g is lost to slag and handling, so a 100g bar yields roughly 98g.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature for preheating a mold?
quiz.explanation: Preheating to 200Â°C removes moisture and prevents splattering.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a well-poured gold bar?
options: A) Smooth surface and sharp edges
quiz.explanation: A smooth surface and sharp edges indicate proper pouring and cooling.

quiz.q: What should you do if your gold melt looks too thick?
options: A) Add more borax and reheat
quiz.explanation: Adding a pinch of borax and reheating improves flow.

quiz.q: Why is it important to work with a partner when pouring gold?
options: B) To have someone call for help in an accident
quiz.explanation: A partner can assist and seek help if an accident occurs.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
quiz.explanation: Safety gear must be worn before any other step in the pouring process.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of stamping a gold bar?
options: A) To make it look pretty
B) To indicate weight and purity for buyers
quiz.explanation: Stamping provides essential information that buyers require for valuation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mistake when pouring gold?
quiz.explanation: Too much borax makes the gold thick and difficult to pour.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio of borax to gold for a 50g button?
quiz.explanation: Using 5g per 100g, a 50g button needs 2.5g of borax.

quiz.q: What should you do if your gold bar has bubbles?
quiz.explanation: Bubbles indicate pouring too fast or a cold mold; re-melting and re-pouring fixes it.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important in gold smelting?
options: A) To keep the room cool
C) To make the gold melt faster
quiz.explanation: Smelting releases toxic fumes that must be vented to avoid health problems.

quiz.q: What is the best way to clean a gold bar after pouring?
options: A) Scrub with wire brush and soapy water
quiz.explanation: Wire brushing with soapy water removes borax residue and gives a clean finish.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice for quality pouring?
options: A) Pour on a wet surface
B) Use a clean, dry mold
quiz.explanation: A clean, dry mold prevents contamination and explosions.

quiz.q: What should you do if your crucible has a crack?
quiz.explanation: A cracked crucible can spill molten gold, causing injury and loss.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pouring distance from crucible to mold?
quiz.explanation: Pouring close to the mold minimizes splashing and oxidation.

quiz.q: What should you do after completing the practical exercise?
options: A) Record the results in a logbook
quiz.explanation: Recording results helps track progress and improve future pours.
